claims.text: The patient presented on 07/01/26 with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden 'thunderclap' onset following physical exertion, characterized as throbbing and diffuse with associated mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, or neck stiffness.
The patient reported no past medical history, no current medications, and no known allergies.

Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, engages in regular jogging, denies smoking or recreational drug use, and consumes approximately 6 units of alcohol per week.
Family history is negative for cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, or migraines in the immediate family, though the mother has type 2 diabetes and the father has hypertension.

Initial triage and examination on 07/01/26 recorded a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg, heart rate of 88 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, temperature of 36.7-36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air.

Initial neurological examination on 07/01/26 was unremarkable, showing the patient alert and oriented with no focal neurological deficits, normal cranial nerves, normal motor and sensory function, no neck stiffness, and unremarkable fundoscopy.
A CT head scan performed at 14:45 on 07/01/26 showed no evidence of intracranial haemorrhage or mass lesion.
Blood tests collected at 15:15 on 07/01/26 revealed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L) interpreted as non-infectious, CRP of 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function tests.
On 07/01/26, the diagnosis of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) was suspected based on clinical presentation and CT findings, and the patient was admitted to the Neurology ward.
On 07/01/26, oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours was initiated to manage vasospasm.
On 07/01/26, the patient's headache persisted at 7/10 intensity, blood pressure was 150/92 mmHg, and blood tests showed mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and marginally elevated CRP (12 mg/L).
On 07/01/26, oral potassium chloride 1 g twice daily was added to the regimen to correct hypokalemia.
The patient's GP was contacted at 20:00 on 07/01/26 to provide an update on admission and the preliminary diagnosis of RCVS.
On 08/01/26, MRI/MRA confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS, the headache severity reduced to 5/10, blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg, CRP was 12 mg/L, and mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) persisted.
On 08/01/26, the nimodipine dose was reduced to 30 mg every 4 hours, and a repeat MRA was planned for 48 hours later to assess resolution.
On 08/01/26, the patient received education on RCVS, including the importance of avoiding triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, triptans, and ergotamines.
On 09/01/26, the headache severity further reduced to 3/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and blood tests from 08/01/26 showed mild hyponatremia (sodium 132 mmol/L).
On 09/01/26, the plan included increasing oral sodium intake through dietary measures and restricting excessive fluid intake to correct hyponatremia, with a repeat MRA scheduled for 24 hours later.
On 09/01/26, the rehab team assessed the patient and noted mild residual neck stiffness with no significant functional impairments, deciding to arrange outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge.
On 10/01/26, the headache intensity was 2/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and the patient remained on nimodipine 30 mg every 4 hours with dietary management for hyponatremia.
On 10/01/26, a repeat MRA was planned for 11/01/26, and the patient was provided with a discharge planning booklet covering RCVS management, lifestyle modifications, and warning signs.
On 11/01/26, the patient reported headache intensity of 2/10 with no new neurological symptoms, and blood pressure was 125/78 mmHg.
A repeat MRA performed at 10:30 on 11/01/26 showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction, confirming the diagnosis of RCVS.
On 11/01/26, discharge was planned for 12/01/26, and outpatient neurology follow-up was arranged for 4 weeks post-discharge.
On 12/01/26, the patient reported no further headaches, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, and the repeat MRA from 11/01/26 confirmed resolution of vasoconstriction.

On 12/01/26, the discharge plan included nimodipine 30 mg orally four times daily to be tapered over 2 weeks, referral for neurology outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks, and advice to avoid known triggers.

On 12/01/26, the GP was contacted to discuss discharge, during which a discharge medication of amlodipine 5 mg once daily was discussed, conflicting with the nimodipine regimen documented in the ward round.
